title: Separation Techniques 2: Textbook
subject: Chemistry
description: Textbook questions on mixtures vs compounds, purity, solubility, filtration, crystallisation, distillation and chromatography.
author: L.M.

cards.front: In a MIXTURE of iron and sulfur, what happens to the properties of each substance?
cards.back:
They keep their own properties

(In a mixture, each substance keeps its own properties. You can still see yellow sulfur and shiny grey iron, and the iron is still magnetic.)

cards.front: How do the AMOUNTS of substances differ in a mixture and in a compound?
cards.back:
In a mixture you can change the amounts; in a compound the relative amounts are fixed

(You can add more sand or less salt to a mixture. But a compound always has the same ratio, e.g. water is always H₂O.)

cards.front: How would you split iron sulfide (a compound) back into iron and sulfur?
cards.back:
You need a chemical reaction

(The atoms are chemically joined, so physical methods like magnets won't work. Only a chemical reaction can split a compound.)

cards.front: Shilpa heats stearic acid. Sample X stays at 70 °C until it's all melted. Sample Y melts between 70 °C and 80 °C. Which is pure?
cards.back:
Sample X, because it has a sharp melting point

(A pure substance melts at one exact temperature [flat line]. Y melts over a range, so it's impure.)

cards.front: What does the word PURE mean in chemistry?
cards.back:
It has no other substances mixed with it

(Pure means only one substance. 'Pure' orange juice is actually a mixture in chemistry terms!)

cards.front: What does a solution look like?
cards.back:
All parts of the mixture are the same and you can't see the separate substances

(A solution is a liquid mixed with a solid or gas, and it looks the same all the way through.)

cards.front: How do we know a solute hasn't disappeared when it dissolves?
cards.back:
The mass of the solution = mass of solute + mass of solvent

(Mass is conserved. Also some solutions are coloured [copper sulfate is blue], showing the solute is still there.)

cards.front: Sarah dissolves 3 g of copper sulfate in 100 g of water. What is the mass of the solution?
cards.back:
103 g

(Just add them: 100 g + 3 g = 103 g.)
cards.hint: Nothing is lost when it dissolves.

cards.front: Using the particle model, what happens when sugar dissolves in water?
cards.back:
Water particles surround each sugar particle, and they mix randomly

(Solvent particles surround the solute particles. Dissolving is NOT melting – a common exam mistake!)

cards.front: Nail varnish doesn't dissolve in water. What is nail-varnish remover mainly made of?
cards.back:
Propanone

(Water isn't the only solvent. Propanone and ethanol are solvents too.)

cards.front: What makes fizzy drinks fizzy?
cards.back:
Dissolved carbon dioxide gas

(Gases can dissolve too. When you open the bottle, the carbon dioxide leaves the solution.)

cards.front: What is the textbook's definition of SOLUBILITY?
cards.back:
The mass of solute that dissolves in 100 g of water to make a saturated solution

(Learn the '100 g of water' part – exams love it. Every substance has its own solubility.)

cards.front: At 20 °C, 202 g of sugar or 36 g of salt dissolves in 100 g of water. Which is more soluble?
cards.back:
Sugar

(The bigger the mass that dissolves in 100 g of water, the more soluble it is.)

cards.front: How can you tell a solution is saturated just by looking at it?
cards.back:
There is undissolved solid at the bottom

(Extra solute can't dissolve, so it just falls to the bottom.)

cards.front: Sugar's solubility goes from 202 g to 476 g between 20 °C and 100 °C. Salt only goes from 36 g to 39 g. What does this show?
cards.back:
Most substances get more soluble when hotter, but by different amounts

(Both increase, but sugar's solubility increases far more than salt's.)

cards.front: Cerium(III) sulfate: 21 g dissolves at 0 °C but only 4 g at 60 °C. What's unusual?
cards.back:
It gets LESS soluble as temperature rises

(Most solids get more soluble when hot, but not all! This is the exception from the end-of-chapter question.)

cards.front: Which two substances does the textbook give as INSOLUBLE in water?
cards.back:
Chalk and sand

(Chalk [calcium carbonate] and sand [silicon dioxide] don't dissolve in water.)

cards.front: Naomi adds 100 g of four compounds to 100 g of water, then filters. Which is MOST soluble? (Residues: calcium chloride 25 g, calcium hydrogen carbonate 84 g, calcium bromide 0 g, calcium iodide 33 g)
cards.back:
Calcium bromide

(Least residue left = most dissolved. Calcium bromide left 0 g, so all 100 g dissolved. Calcium hydrogen carbonate [84 g left] is the least soluble.)
cards.hint: Less left in the filter paper = more dissolved.

cards.front: Filtration separates a liquid from an insoluble solid. What else can it separate?
cards.back:
A solution from a solid that is mixed with it but not dissolved

(E.g. salt solution passes through the paper, while undissolved sand stays behind.)

cards.front: Martha filters a mixture of glitter and water. Name the filtrate and the residue.
cards.back:
Filtrate = water, residue = glitter

(Water passes through [filtrate]; glitter is too big for the holes, so it stays behind [residue].)

cards.front: Name some uses of filtration from the textbook.
cards.back:
Making coffee, oil filters in cars, sand filters for drinking water, the LifeStraw

(Filtration can NOT get salt from seawater: the salt is dissolved, so you need evaporation.)

cards.front: When making copper sulfate crystals, how do you get BIGGER crystals?
cards.back:
Let the water evaporate slowly

(The more slowly the water evaporates, the bigger the crystals.)

cards.front: What is DISTILLATION?
cards.back:
Using evaporation and condensation to get the solvent from a solution

(Distillation collects the SOLVENT [e.g. pure water]. Evaporation keeps the SOLUTE [e.g. salt].)

cards.front: In distillation apparatus, what does the CONDENSER do?
cards.back:
Cools the steam so it turns back into liquid water

(Cold water flows around the condenser, cooling the steam so it condenses and drips into the beaker.)

cards.front: What is the correct order for distilling salty water?
cards.back:
Water boils → steam leaves → steam cools in condenser → condenses → drips into beaker

(Heat, boil, steam travels into the condenser, cools, condenses, pure water drips into the beaker. The salt stays in the flask.)

cards.front: You want propanone (the solvent) back out of nail-varnish remover. Which method?
cards.back:
Distillation, because you want the solvent

(Rule: want the SOLVENT [liquid] → distillation. Want the SOLUTE [solid crystals] → evaporation.)

cards.front: Chromatography only works if the substances in the mixture are…
cards.back:
All soluble in the same solvent

(The solvent has to dissolve the dyes to carry them up the paper.)

cards.front: Why do some dyes travel further up the chromatography paper than others?
cards.back:
They are more soluble, or stick less strongly to the paper

(More soluble dyes get carried further by the solvent; dyes that stick strongly to the paper stay lower.)

cards.front: Name some uses of chromatography from the textbook.
cards.back: Comparing vitamin A in types of cassava, separating pigments in spinach, dyes in sweet coatings, detectives testing for explosives

cards.front: Milly dissolves different masses of salt in 100 g of water to see if a golf ball floats. What is the INDEPENDENT variable?
cards.back:
The mass of salt

(She changes the mass of salt [independent]. She observes whether the ball floats [dependent]. She keeps the mass of water and the golf ball the same [control].)

cards.front: The ball first floats when 20 g of salt is dissolved in 100 g of water. How much salt would she need for 200 g of water?
cards.back:
40 g

(Double the water, so double the salt to get the same concentration: 2 × 20 g = 40 g.)
